It appears the Charter retrieval tools are currently returning no results (I tried a search, a title listing, and a section lookup without success), so I can't pull the exact statutory text for you right now. Based on my general knowledge of the New York City Charter (you can verify the current text at codelibrary.amlegal.com), the Public Advocate's powers are set out primarily in Chapter 2 of the Charter (§§ 21–25) and include:

**Charter § 24 — Duties of the Public Advocate:**
- Serves as an ombudsman for City government — receives, investigates, and seeks to resolve complaints from individuals and communities about City services, agencies, and operations.
- Handles complaints referred from other offices, including those from the 311 system.
- Provides reports to the public about City agency service delivery and performance.

**Charter § 25 — Additional duties:**
- Appoints a member of the New York City Board of Education (now Panel for Educational Policy).
- Sits as a member of various boards and commissions by virtue of the office.

**Other Charter provisions:**
- The Public Advocate is a citywide elected official (Charter § 21), next in line of succession to the mayor (after the Mayor and, historically, the City Council President role was merged — the Public Advocate is first in line if the Mayor cannot serve).
- The Public Advocate is a member of the City Council's legislative process in limited ways and, under the City Council Rules, presides over Council meetings in the absence of the Speaker (a Council rule, not the Charter itself).
- The office also sponsors and proposes legislation (through its City Council seat) and appoints members to certain boards (e.g., one member of the City Planning Commission? — no; the Planning Commission member is appointed by the Borough Presidents and the Speaker — the Public Advocate appoints a member of the PEP).

In short: the Charter gives the Public Advocate a citywide investigative and ombudsman role — resolving complaints about City services, monitoring agency performance, reporting to the public, and holding a position in mayoral succession — but no direct control over any City agency's operations.

I'd recommend checking the official text (Charter Chapter 2, §§ 21–25) at codelibrary.amlegal.com, since my sources here couldn't be retrieved live to confirm the exact current wording.
